---
title: "Confidence Intervals in Meta-analysis"
---

@fig-meta-analysis below shows an example of how confidence intervals are used 
in everyday research. Meta-analysis is the field that combines the results of 
multiple research papers/studies to better understand what's going on in the 
population (i.e. the unknown population parameter of interest).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-meta-analysis
#| fig-cap: "An example of how confidence intervals are used in meta-analysis."
#| fig-alt: "A forest plot showing the results of a meta-analysis with confidence intervals for each study."

knitr::include_graphics("https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-73773-2_2/MediaObjects/536349_1_En_2_Fig1_HTML.png")
```

Each paper/study is represented as a row and is labelled by the authors' 
surnames and year of publication. Each study published a point estimate of the 
unknown population parameter (the diamond) and a confidence interval 
(CI, the horizontal line). 

All studies are trying to estimate the unknown population parameter, and each 
returned a different estimate and CI. By looking at the various estimates from 
multiple studies, we can gain a better understanding of what the true population 
parameter might be.

In the "overall' row at the bottom of the table, you see a diamond and 
horizontal line that tries to summarise the combined results of all the studies 
included in the meta-analysis. The idea is that the combined results of all the 
studies will give us a better estimate of the unknown population parameter than 
any single study could on its own. The diamond represents the overall effect 
size, while the horizontal line represents the confidence interval for that 
effect size. You will learn more about the term "effect size" in the next 
semester and for now you can think of it as a measure of the strength of the 
relationship between two variables. How meta-analysis combines the results from 
different studies into an "overall" estimate and CI is beyond the scope of this 
course, but you will see more meta-analyses as you go through your Psychology 
degree.


## References

Ashford, S., Edmunds, J., & French, D. P. (2010). What is the best way to 
change self-efficacy to promote lifestyle and recreational physical activity? 
A systematic review with meta-analysis. British Journal of Health Psychology, 
15(2), 265–288. https://doi.org/10.1348/135910709X461752
